defs: A memory-safety flaw where more data is written into a buffer than it was designed to hold.
Ensuring data stays accurate, complete, and protected from unauthorized modification.

course.learn: Application vulnerabilities are flaws in software design, coding, input handling, authentication, authorization, or memory management that attackers can exploit.
course.why: Applications directly process untrusted input and sensitive data, making secure coding and testing essential.
course.example: A web application builds SQL statements by concatenating user input, allowing an attacker to alter the query.
course.exam: Know common web/app flaws such as injection, XSS, broken access control, race conditions, and buffer overflows.

course.learn: Operating-system vulnerabilities include missing patches, weak permissions, kernel flaws, insecure services, authentication weaknesses, and configuration errors.
course.why: The OS is the foundation for applications and hardware access; compromise can give an attacker broad control.
course.example: An unpatched privilege-escalation flaw lets a local user gain administrator/root rights.
course.exam: Patch and harden where possible; legacy or unsupported systems may require isolation and compensating controls.

slides.raw:
Web-based Vulnerabilities

slides.teach: A vulnerability is a weakness. For each item, connect the weakness to its likely impact and the best mitigation.
defs: Cross-Site Request Forgery: tricks an authenticated browser into sending an unwanted request.
Insecure Direct Object Reference: an authorization flaw where changing an object identifier exposes another user’s resource.
Cross-Site Scripting: malicious client-side script executes in another user’s browser.

course.learn: Web applications face vulnerabilities in input handling, authentication, sessions, authorization, file uploads, security headers, and XML processing. Common examples include XSS, SQL injection, CSRF, IDOR, and XXE.
course.why: Web applications are exposed to untrusted users and often connect directly to sensitive data or backend services.
course.example: A site correctly authenticates users but fails to check object ownership, allowing one user to change an ID in the URL and read another user's record.
course.exam: Identify the layer: SQLi = database query, XSS = browser script, CSRF = unwanted authenticated request, IDOR = broken object authorization, XXE = XML parser.

breakdown.explanation: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) lets attacker-controlled script execute in another user's browser in the context of a trusted site.
SQL injection changes a database query by inserting malicious SQL through application input. Prepared/parameterized queries keep user data separate from SQL syntax.
Forgery creates or alters data, documents, messages, tokens, or transactions so they appear legitimate when they are not.

course.learn: Hardware security risk includes vulnerable firmware, malicious peripherals, insecure interfaces, unsupported devices, and physical tampering.
course.why: Software controls can be undermined if the underlying hardware or firmware is compromised.
course.example: An attacker installs a malicious USB device that impersonates a keyboard and injects commands.
course.exam: Hardware/firmware threats often require physical security, signed firmware, inventory, secure boot, or device control.

defs: Using a hypervisor to run multiple virtual machines, usually with separate guest operating systems, on shared hardware.

course.learn: Virtualization adds a hypervisor and isolation boundary between workloads. Weaknesses include VM escape, hypervisor compromise, poor isolation, and resource exhaustion.
course.why: One hypervisor may host many critical systems, so a virtualization-layer flaw can have a large blast radius.
course.example: A VM escape vulnerability lets code inside one guest reach the host and potentially other VMs.
course.exam: VM escape/hypervisor = virtualization clue. Containers share the host kernel and have different isolation tradeoffs.

course.learn: Cloud vulnerabilities often come from excessive IAM permissions, exposed storage, insecure APIs, weak secrets, poor logging, and misunderstanding the shared-responsibility model.
course.why: Cloud resources can be Internet-accessible in seconds, so one configuration mistake can expose large amounts of data.
course.example: A storage bucket containing customer exports is accidentally configured for public read access.
course.exam: Public bucket, over-privileged role, leaked API key, or insecure cloud API usually points to cloud misconfiguration/IAM.

course.learn: Cryptographic vulnerabilities arise from weak algorithms, poor random-number generation, bad key management, implementation flaws, side channels, and insecure protocol choices.
course.why: Even mathematically strong cryptography can fail when implemented or operated incorrectly.
course.example: An application generates predictable session keys because its random-number source has very low entropy.
course.exam: Look beyond the algorithm name: key storage, entropy, protocol downgrade, and implementation details matter.

course.learn: Mobile-device risk comes from outdated operating systems, excessive app permissions, malicious or sideloaded apps, insecure wireless networks, device loss, rooting/jailbreaking, and weak data protection.
course.why: Mobile devices combine sensitive data, identity tokens, cameras, radios, and physical portability in one easily lost endpoint.
course.example: A user sideloads an untrusted app that requests access to contacts, SMS, microphone, and accessibility services.
course.exam: Use MDM/UEM, encryption, screen lock, approved app stores, patching, remote wipe, least privilege, and network protections.

breakdown.explanation: System monitoring focuses on endpoints and hosts. Endpoint Protection Platforms (EPP) detect or prevent malicious endpoint activity, while SIEM platforms collect and correlate events from many systems.
Permissions define the actions a subject may perform on a resource, such as read, write, execute, modify, or administer. They are one mechanism used to implement authorization.

slides.title: Zero Day
slides.raw:
Zero Day
No Prior Awareness
Rapid Exploitation
No Signatures
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: A zero-day is a vulnerability for which defenders do not yet have an effective fix available or widely deployed while attackers may already be able to exploit it.
course.why: Organizations cannot rely on patching alone, so they must reduce exposure using segmentation, detection, isolation, allow listing, or other compensating controls.
course.example: A critical browser flaw is exploited in the wild before the vendor releases a patch, so the company temporarily disables the affected feature and increases monitoring.
course.exam: If no patch exists, choose risk-reduction controls rather than “install the patch.”
